summary: Hebrew marks a definite noun with the prefix ha- (הַ), written attached to the noun and to every adjective that agrees with it (הַבָּצָל הַיָּרֹק). There is no indefinite article: a bare noun is indefinite (גֶּזֶר “a carrot / carrots”). A definite direct object is introduced by אֶת (הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת הַגֶּזֶר). The article usually doubles the next consonant with a dagesh (הַשּׁוּם, הַכְּרוּב); before the gutturals, which cannot be doubled, its vowel changes: הָ before א, ע, ר (הָעַגְבָנִיָּה, הָאֲפוּנָה), הַ with no doubling before ה and ח (הַחַסָּה, הַחֲצִילִים), and הֶ before חָ (הֶחָצִיל, הֶחָרִיף).

askYourself: Is the thing specific — already known to the listener, or the only one? → add הַ.
What is the first letter of the noun? א / ע / ר → הָ; ה / ח → הַ without a dagesh; חָ → הֶ; any other letter → הַ + a dagesh in that letter.
Is there an adjective after the noun? It takes the article too: הַפִּלְפֵּל הֶחָרִיף.
Is the definite noun the direct object of the verb? → put אֶת before it.
Is it a construct phrase (two nouns, like תַּפּוּחַ אֲדָמָה)? → the article goes on the last noun: תַּפּוּחַ הָאֲדָמָה.
steps: Choose the form of the article from the first letter.
Repeat the article on agreeing adjectives.
Add אֶת if it is a definite direct object.

traps: No indefinite article: “a tomato” is just עַגְבָנִיָּה — never *אַחַת עַגְבָנִיָּה as an article.
אֶת only before a definite object: הוּא אוֹכֵל בָּצָל (no אֶת), but הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת הַבָּצָל.
The article changes before gutturals: הָעַגְבָנִיָּה, הֶחָצִיל — but the plural הַחֲצִילִים, because there the ח has a hataf patah, not a qamats.
In a noun–adjective phrase both words take the article: הַבָּצָל הַיָּרֹק, not *הַבָּצָל יָרֹק (that means “the onion is green”).
Names and nouns with a possessive suffix are already definite and take no הַ.
